questions.q: Grace has no tasks. What happens to her in select users.name, tasks.title from users join tasks on tasks.user_id = users.id?
questions.explain: An inner join (join) keeps only pairs that match. Grace has no matching task, so she disappears. A left join would keep her with null on the task side.
options: She does not appear at all
The query fails, because a user without tasks breaks the join
She appears once for every task in the table

questions.q: What does a left join do?
questions.explain: The left table is the one after from. Use a left join whenever "nothing on the right" is an answer you still want to see.
options: It keeps only the rows of the right table
It keeps every row of the left table; where nothing matches on the right, the right side's columns are null
It joins the tables in reverse order
It is the same as an inner join, but faster

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Grace has no task, so the task columns of her row are null in SQL, and null in JavaScript too, not undefined or an empty string.
options: [ { name: 'Ada', title: 'Buy milk' }, { name: 'Grace', title: null } ]
[ { name: 'Ada', title: 'Buy milk' }, { name: 'Grace', title: undefined } ]

questions.q: The "open task" condition is in the where this time. What does this print?
questions.explain: For Grace, t.done is null, and not null is not true, so the where throws her row away: the left join acts like an inner join. Conditions on the right table of a left join belong in the on.

questions.q: You want every user, with their open tasks if they have any. Where does not t.done go in from users u left join tasks t on t.user_id = u.id?
questions.explain: In the on, the condition only decides which tasks match; users without an open task are still kept. In a where, it removes those users' rows, which is a classic mistake.
options: In the on: on t.user_id = u.id and not t.done

questions.q: What are u and t in from users u left join tasks t on t.user_id = u.id?
questions.explain: An alias is a short name for a table inside one query. t.user_id means the user_id column of tasks.
options: New tables that the query creates
Short aliases for the tables, to save typing

questions.q: Grace has no tasks. What does this print?
questions.explain: The left join gives Grace one row with t.id as null. count(t.id) counts only non-null values (0); count(*) counts rows (1).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: avg returns the exact decimal type numeric, which the driver hands over as a string so no digits are lost. Round it in SQL and cast it with ::float8 when you want a JavaScript number.

questions.q: Why does the driver hand numeric values (such as the result of avg) to JavaScript as strings?
questions.explain: numeric is exact and can have many digits; a JavaScript number cannot hold them all. Both pg and PGlite return numeric as a string. The same reason makes pg return bigint values, such as counts, as strings.
options: Because PostgreSQL stores all numbers as text
Because a JavaScript number could lose digits of an exact decimal
Because the driver has a bug that will be fixed

questions.q: PostgreSQL refuses select u.name, t.title, count(t.id) from users u join tasks t on t.user_id = u.id group by u.id, u.name. Why?
questions.explain: Each group becomes one row. A user with three tasks has three titles, so every selected column must either be grouped or be summarised by an aggregate.
options: You cannot use count with a join
t.title is neither inside an aggregate nor listed in group by, so PostgreSQL does not know which title to show
A query can only group by one column

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: group by splits the rows per user and every aggregate runs once per group. filter (where done) makes count look only at the done rows; sum still adds all estimates of the group.

questions.q: What is the difference between where and having?
questions.explain: "Users with more than an hour of work" needs sum(...), which only exists after grouping, so it goes in having. "Only open tasks" is a row filter, so it goes in where.
options: They are the same; having is the older spelling
where filters rows before grouping; having filters groups after grouping, so it can use aggregates
having filters rows before grouping; where filters groups
where works only on numbers; having works on text

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: where first drops Alan's done task, so his open work is exactly 60, which is not more than 60. Ada has 140 and Grace 75 minutes open.

questions.q: Why may order by use the alias open_minutes, while having must repeat sum(t.estimate)?
questions.explain: The order is: from and joins, where, group by, having, select, order by, limit. An alias exists only once select has run.
options: Because having does not allow any names
PostgreSQL works through having before select (where the alias is made) and order by after it
Because aliases only work on text columns
It is a bug in PostgreSQL

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The subquery produces one value: the average estimate, 60. The outer query keeps tasks above it, so Fix bike at exactly 60 is not included.

questions.q: What makes a subquery correlated?
questions.explain: In where not exists (select 1 from tasks t where t.user_id = u.id ...), the subquery uses u.id from the outer query, so it asks its question once per user.
options: It returns more than one column
It refers to a column of the outer query, so it runs for each outer row

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The question per user is "does this user have any open task?". Ada does. Alan's only task is done, and Grace has no tasks at all, so both have no open task.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Inside the transaction the delete really happened, so the count is 2. rollback throws away every change since begin, and all five rows are back.

questions.q: What does commit do?
questions.explain: begin starts a transaction, commit saves all of its changes together, and rollback undoes all of them.
options: Saves every change since begin, all at once

questions.q: With the pg package and a Pool, how do you run a transaction correctly?
questions.explain: A transaction belongs to one connection. Two pool.query calls may use two different connections, so begin and your update could end up in different places.
options: Call pool.query("begin"), then your queries with pool.query, then pool.query("commit")
Take one client with pool.connect(), run begin, your queries and commit on that client, and release() it at the end
Create a new Pool for every transaction
Transactions are not possible with a pool

questions.q: What is the difference between explain and explain analyze?
questions.explain: Because explain analyze really runs the query, be careful with it in front of an update or delete: the change happens too.
options: explain analyze only shows the plan; explain runs the query
explain only shows the plan; explain analyze really runs the query and reports what happened, including the time

questions.q: A slow endpoint's plan shows Seq Scan on tasks with Rows Removed by Filter: 199934 to return 66 rows. What is the likely fix?
questions.explain: The database read the whole table to keep a few rows. An index on the filtered columns lets it find those rows directly.
options: Add an index on the columns the query filters by

questions.q: There is an index on tasks (user_id, done). Which query can it serve well?
questions.explain: A composite index is sorted by its first column, then its second. It helps queries on the leading column (user_id), with or without done, but not queries on done alone.
options: where user_id = 42 and not done, and also where user_id = 42 alone
Only queries that filter by done first
No query, until you also index done alone

questions.q: Does the planner use the index? What does this print?
questions.explain: With an index on (user_id, done) the planner finds the few matching rows through the index instead of a Seq Scan over 20,000 rows.

questions.q: Why does a server use a connection pool?
questions.explain: A pool reuses open connections. A server keeps it for its whole life; a script calls pool.end() so it can exit.
options: To run every query twice for safety
Opening a new connection for every request is slow, so the pool keeps a few open and lends one to each query
Because PostgreSQL allows only one connection
To store query results in memory

questions.q: Where should the connection URL postgres://user:password@host:port/database come from?
questions.explain: The location is configuration and the password is a secret, so neither belongs in your code. Failing fast with a clear message beats connecting to the wrong place.
options: A constant at the top of tasks.js, committed with the code
The DATABASE_URL environment variable, and the program refuses to start without it
A query-string parameter on each request

questions.q: With pg, select count(*) as n from tasks gives { n: '2' }. Why a string?
questions.explain: Write count(*)::int when you know the number is small, or convert with Number(...). PGlite behaves differently: it returns a JavaScript number when the value fits safely (up to 253 − 1) and a JavaScript bigint beyond that, which is why the PGlite examples print plain numbers.
options: count returns a 64-bit bigint, which can be larger than a JavaScript number can hold exactly
Because pg returns every column as a string
Because as n turns the value into text

questions.q: SQL's coalesce is like JavaScript's ??. What does this print?
questions.explain: ?? and coalesce replace only a missing value (null). || also replaces 0, which is a real answer: a user with 0 minutes of work is not "none".
questions.code:
const minutes = [null, 0, 150];
console.log(minutes.map((m) => m ?? 0), minutes.map((m) => m || "none"));

questions.q: A group with no rows has no average. What does this JavaScript print?
questions.explain: Dividing 0 by 0 gives NaN. SQL is more honest here: sum and avg of no rows are null, which you then handle on purpose, for example with coalesce.

questions.q: pg returned the count as the string '2'. What does this print?
questions.explain: + with a string joins text, so "2" + 1 is "21". Convert with Number (or cast with ::int in SQL) before doing maths.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A connection URL has the form postgres://user:password@host:port/database. The password sits inside it, which is why the whole URL is a secret that lives in the environment.
questions.code:
const url = new URL("postgres://postgres:s3cret@localhost:5434/taskdb");
console.log(url.username, url.hostname, url.port, url.pathname);

questions.q: node tasks.js fails with password authentication failed for user "postgres". What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: The URL is built from PGPASSWORD. In a new terminal window that variable is empty, so the URL carries a wrong password.
options: The password in DATABASE_URL does not match the server's (for example, PGPASSWORD was not set in this terminal)
The query has a syntax error

questions.q: Do in JavaScript what select user_id, count(*) from tasks group by user_id does. Finish countByUser so it returns an object mapping each userId to its number of tasks.
questions.explain: Each group is a key, and the aggregate (here a count) is updated once per row. Object keys are strings, so Node prints them in quotes.

questions.q: Do a left join in JavaScript. Finish leftJoin(users, tasks): for every user, one row { name, title } per task of theirs, or a single row with title: null when they have none. Keep the users' order.
questions.explain: An inner join would drop Grace. The left join keeps every left row and fills the right side with null when nothing matches.

questions.q: Do where not done ... group by owner having sum(estimate) > 60 in JavaScript. Finish busyOwners: skip done tasks, add up the estimates per owner, and return the owners whose total is more than limit, in the order they first appear.
questions.explain: First filter rows (where), then group and sum, then filter the groups (having). Alan's open total is exactly 60, which is not more than 60.

questions.q: Write coalesce(...values) like SQL's: return the first value that is not null or undefined, or null if there is none. Note that 0 and "" are real values.
questions.explain: Check for null/undefined only, not for falsy values: a sum of 0 minutes is a real answer. That is also the difference between ?? and || in JavaScript.

questions.q: Finish average(estimates): like round(avg(estimate), 1), return the average rounded to one decimal, as a number. For an empty list return null, just as avg of no rows is null.
questions.explain: An empty group has no average, so null is more honest than 0 or NaN. Multiply by 10, round, and divide by 10 to keep one decimal.

questions.q: Finish withTransaction(pool, work) the way the lesson describes for pg: take one client with await pool.connect(), run begin, call work(client), then commit. If work throws, run rollback and throw the error again. Always release() the client. The fake pool below logs every call.
questions.explain: Every statement of the transaction runs on the same client. finally releases it whether the work succeeded or failed; a client that is never released is lost from the pool.
questions.expected:
connect, begin, update tasks set done = true, commit, release
connect, begin, rollback, release, error: check failed

questions.q: Finish databaseUrl(env). If env.DATABASE_URL is missing or empty, throw an Error with the message DATABASE_URL is not set. Otherwise return it.
questions.explain: Configuration comes from the environment, never from a default hidden in the code. Failing at start-up with a clear message is much easier to debug than a connection error later.
questions.expected:
refused: DATABASE_URL is not set
refused: DATABASE_URL is not set
using postgres://app@db:5432/tasks

questions.q: You want to log which database the app uses, but the URL contains the password. Finish redact(url): replace the password between : and @ with ***. A URL without a password stays the same. Use a regular expression.
questions.explain: The password is a secret, and logs are read by many people and tools. Keep the parts that help debugging (user, host, port, database) and hide the rest.
